title: Shifting the fee mix from hours toward fixed, hybrid and outcome-linked fees
problem: When AI shortens a task an hourly bill earns less for the same result, yet about 90% of legal dollars still flow through hourly arrangements.
approach: Firm leaders set a target mix of pricing models across the portfolio rather than deal by deal.
McKinsey says about a quarter of its global fees come from outcomes-based pricing (self-reported); Keypoint Law expects hybrid fees, known part fixed.
Leadership sets the mix; pricing leads and partners set each price, and agree an outcome scorecard with clients.

title: Modelling how much AI compresses each type of work before rate setting
problem: Firms set rates and fee arrangements on averages, without a view of which work AI will shorten, while rates and results are moving apart.
approach: Legal Decoder said it would release a tool sorting legal work into eight archetypes with expected AI compression, plus a pricing builder.
Recruiter postings for unnamed global firms ask pricing staff to model margins for AI-assisted matters. No firm describes using the modelling.
Pricing or finance leadership reviews assumptions before rates change, and partners review work clusters before they become fee schedules.

title: Using captured work data to find revenue leakage and manage matter profitability
problem: Firms learn that a matter lost money after the bill is out; recorded time differs from time worked, and fixed-fee delivery cost is a guess.
approach: Laurel captures activity across applications, drafts time entries, and shows recorded versus actual time, cost against revenue and leverage as work runs.
Tonkon Torp reports 21 minutes a day per lawyer and 20% faster collection (vendor-published); Aprio and Bonadio Group are cited.
Timekeepers review drafted entries; finance and practice leaders review flags, and partners decide pricing and staffing.
who: Tonkon Torp, Aprio, Bonadio Group, Laurel

title: Analysing every line of legal bills with machine learning to police fees
problem: Billing codes are unreliable, so finding block billing or excessive time means reading narratives, and reviewers sample invoices rather than read every line.
approach: Legal Decoder re-categorises every line item from its narrative and applies 45 flags; its Aperture layer answers plain-language questions.
Fee examiners in 4 named bankruptcy cases disclose the tool as their methodology (vendor-published); client names are tokenised before the language model.
Users check findings against invoices by export, and legal operations or the fee examiner decides what to dispute.
who: Legal Decoder, UnitedLex, UBS, fee examiners

title: Finance agents in the billing system explain rates and forecast the ledger
problem: Finance teams spend time assembling context across billing, receivables, time and rate data, and on spreadsheet work to forecast and track rate changes.
approach: Aderant's Agent Center lists a Rates Agent for governed rate requests and a General Ledger Forecasting Agent with variance analysis.
Aderant says agents prepare, prioritise and draft while the team reviews and decides; announced, with no outcomes published.
Rate requests go through governed approvals, and finance staff review forecasts and drafts before use.

title: Aiming AI at the research and drafting time partners write down
problem: Partners write down time that took too long; TRI puts the average partner's own write-downs at about 300 hours a year.
approach: Start with a revenue-leakage analysis to find where hours are lost, then apply AI to those workflows.
A commissioned Forrester study models up to $6.2m over 3 years for a theoretical large firm (vendor-published). No firm reports measured results.
Billing partners decide whether to write down time.

title: Setting a firm-level AI investment budget and reviewing it against finance measures
problem: Spending is ahead of proof: only 18% of professionals say their organisation tracks AI return on investment.
approach: Firms set an AI budget and review spend against adoption and measures leaders already watch, such as utilisation and margin.
PwC reports $3 billion invested across its network in AI and other areas (self-reported); RSM US announced $1 billion over three years.
The executive committee or CFO approves the budget and reviews return measures before renewals.

title: Gating pilot-to-licence decisions on weekly active use on real matters
problem: Lawyers test AI tools on top of billable work, and few legal teams can show a reliable return, so licences risk becoming unused shelfware.
approach: Holland & Hart runs pilots on real matters and treats more than 70% weekly active users as the sign of real adoption.
Laurel Signal and Harvey's Command Center sell usage analytics for this purpose.
A technology lead decides to buy, extend or stop based on trial use; the business owner confirms the goal.

title: Tracking where AI-freed hours go and deciding whether to resell them
problem: AI saves time, but unless freed hours are identified and sold the firm is no more productive; one report calls the gap between time saved and revenue earned the leak.
approach: Advisers tell firms to plan how to reprice or resell saved hours and tie AI to utilisation, margin and revenue per employee.
84.8% of firms say AI saves time (independent); about one third of small law firms are growing revenue from AI (vendor-published).
Practice leaders decide how freed hours are redeployed, and finance reviews revenue and margin per head. No firm describes a tracking system.
who: Vendor claim (SPI, Clio); no firm named

title: Funding a firm-owned AI platform as a multi-year investment, not renting
problem: A firm that only licenses the same AI tools as its rivals has nothing distinctive, and rented tools leave it exposed to vendor pricing changes.
approach: Kirkland & Ellis is building its own platform; Bloomberg Law reports a $500 million commitment, a Palantir relationship and 180+ AI engineers.
Kirkland's figures are self-reported; Ropes & Gray's CIO said building proprietary tools did not appear to make sense for that firm now.
Equity partners take part in AI Pods that define custom builds.

title: Governing AI spend under usage-based pricing: read the meter, set budgets
problem: Firms budgeted per-seat AI fees, but usage-based charges depend on how lawyers prompt and which model they pick, and lawyers cannot see the spend.
approach: At ILTACON 2026, Littler found one PowerPoint cost $2; Barnes & Thornburg saw lawyers choosing the largest model for the smallest task.
Ogletree's chief data and AI officer said firms seem to be settling on AI at roughly 1% of revenue (self-reported).
Knowledge and AI leads review spend by tool and user; finance approves budgets and contract terms.

title: Metering consumption-priced AI by matter and deciding whether to bill clients
problem: Under seat pricing AI could sit in overhead, but agentic tools run many model calls per task, so cost varies by matter and firms must decide who pays.
approach: Legora announced on 2026-06-23 that Agent Pro is priced by consumption, with attribution of every run to a matter and spending controls.
Harvey reports a 14-fold rise in tokens processed in six months (vendor-published). A practitioner opinion recommends absorbing ordinary AI use as overhead.
Finance decides whether to allocate or absorb each AI cost, and the billing partner and client agree terms in the engagement letter.

title: Setting partner expectations, credit and pay rules for AI and non-hourly work
problem: Partners decide billing and staffing, yet only 25% of stand-out lawyers strongly agree their firm has a plan to monetise AI use.
approach: PwC's US chief executive told the FT that partners who resist AI have no place at the firm.
Advisers urge reviewing origination credit and partner pay for value-priced work; Wipfli is introducing client satisfaction and cycle time as staff metrics.
The compensation committee approves metric and credit changes. No firm reports a changed partner pay formula.

title: Idea: modelling leverage and partner income if AI takes over junior work
problem: Idea, not a deployment: associates and non-equity partners carry most of the extra demand while equity-partner demand slipped.
approach: Scenario models of leverage, billing mix and partner income under different assumptions about how much junior and support work AI takes over.
DLA Piper's AI head said some financial-contract due diligence is down to two hours from 15-20. No firm uses such a model.
The executive committee would set associate intake and non-equity partner policy.

title: Accounting firms taking private equity capital to fund talent and technology
problem: Partnerships distribute most profit each year, leaving little capital for technology and talent, and AI productivity cuts revenue under hourly billing.
approach: Crowe announced a KKR investment on 2026-06-11 for talent, technology and innovation, separating attest and non-attest services; it closed in August 2026.
Crowe then launched CroweONE, a shared ownership plan open to all employees. No use of the capital has been published.
Partners vote on the transaction and governance terms, and leadership allocates the capital.

title: Law firms bringing in outside capital for AI through management services organisations
problem: The traditional law-firm structure leaves little cash in reserve while AI platforms need upfront investment, and ABA Model Rule 5.4 bars sharing fees with non-lawyers.
approach: A management services organisation holds the business side so an investor can own it and the law firm pays it fees.
Charlesbank reportedly signed a letter of intent for a Wood Smith Henning & Berman stake; Dudley DeBosier partnered with Orion Legal.
Lawyers keep exclusive control of legal matters; partners approve the agreement and ethics counsel reviews the separation.
who: Wood Smith, Charlesbank, Dudley DeBosier, Orion Legal

title: AI-native firms built around agents and experienced reviewers, not the leverage pyramid
problem: Incumbent economics depend on hourly rates and junior leverage; new entrants claim they can deliver at lower cost without that structure.
approach: General Legal uses a management services structure; six months out of Y Combinator it reports about 400 clients (self-reported).
Norm Law, Arceus and Falcon are cited in law, Queen's Tower Advisory in consulting, and Ascend in accounting.
Experienced lawyers review and answer for agent work (recommended; General Legal's review step is not described).
who: General Legal, Norm Law, Queen's Tower, Ascend
